titles: Evaluation of Enhanced Efficiency Fertilisers: Exploring Next-Gen Fertilisers for Smallholders in Sub-Saharan Africa.
descriptions:
This project, led by the International Fertiliser Development Centre (IFDC), will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of Enhanced Efficiency Fertilisers (EEFs) with a focus on sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The evaluation will benchmark these innovative products against urea, conduct greenhouse evaluations in two contrasting soil types (specifically in soil pH), and carry out field evaluations for different crops and soils in SSA. In addition, the project will further evaluate a selected set of EEFs, chosen based on their performance in laboratory and greenhouse evaluations, through on-farm field trials in two sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries (Tanzania and Zambia). It will also leverage the on-going trials conducted by the USAID-funded IFDC Space to Place Project on improving fertilizer use efficiency in SSA. For example, the Space to Place trials will provide the balanced fertilization requirements for P, K, and secondary and micronutrients thereby ensuring the N response and NUE is not limited by other nutrients. The specific objectives are as follows:

a) Systematic screening of enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers for their nutrient release patterns, transformations, volatilization losses, leaching and nitrous oxide emissions.

b) Screening and field evaluation of enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers for their impact on growth and productivity for various crops on different soils.

c) Development and validation of a Decision Support Tool (DST) for Enhanced Efficiency Nitrogen Fertilizers in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Heart disease and stroke cause the greatest number of deaths in India and are not always identified early enough. Older people are more at risk of these two conditions because they might not get enough physical activity, be overweight, or have high blood pressure or high cholesterol or diabetes. As such, they often face challenges in getting continued care and complying with treatment advice. The project team will work with older people, their caregivers and frontline health workers to design a contextually relevant innovative care package. 
Commencing in  July  2025, the award will deliver four interlinked work packages which will be guided by the community engagement and involvement activities. titles: NIHR Global Health Research Group on the National Confidential Inquiry into suicide deaths, suicide attempts and suicide ideation for India
descriptions:
We aim to set up the National Confidential Inquiry into suicide deaths, suicide ideation and suicide attempts for India (India Inquiry) by adapting the national confidential inquiry into suicide and safety in mental health (NCISH) from the UK to improve data capture and understanding of risk factors to inform suicide prevention and improve services for survivors in India.  This research will focus on understanding of risk factors for suicide deaths from the administrative data at individual-level, and risk factors for suicide ideation and suicide attempt cases from the mental health services, identify gaps in this documentation, and will build consensus on a minimum data requirement and shared operational definitions for risk factors for these data to be utilised to plan, monitor and improve India’s response to suicide prevention.
The project is a collaboration between the University of Manchester (UK), Public Health Foundation of India (New Delhi, India), the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (New Delhi, India), the Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education & Research (Puducherry, India) and the Sisters Living Works (Mumbai, India).  Between July 2024 and June 2028, we will contextually adapt the NCISH as India Inquiry, pilot and refine the India Inquiry approach, test the India Inquiry model in two states, one each in the north and south of India, and then present an adaptable model for use across India.
This project aims to address the high burden of suicide deaths in India.  An estimated 195,000 people died by suicide in 2019 in India, the highest number of suicide deaths globally.  Furthermore, for every death by suicide in India, there are more than 200 people with suicidality and more than 15 suicide attempts.  With the impulsive nature of suicide, and because hanging is increasingly the common method of suicide in India, there is an urgency to act upon suicide prevention.  Suicide is the leading cause of death in the 15-39 age group in India, and the suicide death rate in Indian women is twice that of the global average for women. This research will contribute towards a comprehensive response to suicide prevention in India, which is to ensure that suicide does not continue to cost lives and adversely affect many millions through the loss of loved ones. titles: IndiaZooRisk+: Using OneHealth approaches to understand and co-develop interventions for zoonotic diseases affecting forest communities in India
descriptions: Zoonotic diseases (that spread from animals to humans) disproportionately affect poor tropical communities and can lead to loss of life, impaired livelihoods, health and welfare. Forest habitats are a significant source of such diseases. For communities that depend on forests for food, fuel and income, accessing forests comes with the increased risk of being exposed to zoonotic pathogens. Although we know that zoonotic diseases are increasing globally, we still lack knowledge on how these diseases circulate between wildlife, livestock and people as they use forests, and how environmental changes like forest degradation interact with human migration, local culture and society (knowledge sharing), and policy (land tenure, disease prioritisation) to exacerbate emergence and spread. Focussing on India as a key global hotspot for endemic and emerging zoonotic diseases and bringing together a network of policy makers and practitioners from the human health, animal health and environmental sectors with experts (public and animal health, ecology, epidemiology and social science) - thereby following the One Health approach -, this project aims to reduce health, welfare and livelihood impacts of zoonotic diseases by (1) better understanding the impacts of different drivers on health outcomes and spread of zoonotic diseases (2) co-develop improved interventions, integrating traditional knowledge, with affected forest communities and, thereby building the capacity of local communities to be more resilient to zoonotic diseases. Three neglected zoonotic diseases, Leptospirosis, Kyasanur forest Disease and Scrub Typhus that are widespread across the Western Ghats forest communities and cause severe complications and death if untreated, yet have different transmission routes, will be taken as key case-studies for field research.   The research underpinning these improvements will include: (1) understanding how local culture and policies, nutrition and environment factors affect community interventions, perceptions and health outcomes from zoonotic diseases. (2) investigating how different communities share knowledge on diseases and health intervention, including traditional knowledge, both with each other and with practitioners and managers, to improve communication strategies. (3) studying the role of different wildlife and livestock hosts and tick and mite vectors in transmission of disease to humans in different seasons. (4) understanding how long distance seasonal migration of pastoralists may promote resilience or increase their exposure to diseases and environmental change. (5) developing computer models and risk maps, integrating environmental and social data, for predicting the distribution and spread of diseases. (6) building capacity in research, data analysis and cross-sectoral collaboration to underpin future One Health approaches in India.  Improved decision-support tools and Apps and prioritisation of traditional knowledge will help disease managers, policy makers and community workers to develop novel interventions and better target vaccination and communication efforts towards the communities that are most at risk and help managers in agriculture and environmental sectors to understand how, for these communities, disease impacts may coincide with other negative impacts of environmental change. The project platform and approach of co-developing research, training and decision support tools on zoonotic diseases with stakeholders across sectors, accounting for their needs and underlying ecological and social processes, will build significant capacity in science, policy and practitioners to respond to these emerging and endemic global threats in India and beyond.

titles: NIHR-HSPR-PA- Reimagining the health system from the world view of indigenous communities (rTribe study)
descriptions:
Adivasi communities (indigenous communities in India) are known to have poor access to healthcare and poor health status, often due to social and historical reasons. Healthcare services in Adivasi settings often do not provide care in a way that is acceptable and respectful of their culture and history.
The study will apply state-of-the-art health policy & systems research methods to co-produce knowledge on improving the health system's responsiveness to Adivasi communities in Southern India. Guided by the tenets of indigenous standpoint theory, the study will take a multi-method participatory action research approach to reimagine and co-produce transformative solutions for strengthening health systems' responsiveness in two Adivasi community settings in Southern India. This project will build upon existing, long-term, trust-based collaborative relationships between the research team, Adivasi leaders, community-based organisations, and government decision-makers in two remote, forested Adivasi settings in two states in Southern India. The study team aims to improve the responsiveness of the health system to the needs and expectations of Adivasi communities in these two settings and use the knowledge to build a model of practice that can achieve this in other settings.
The study will be undertaken by Deva Soliga Cultural and Development Trust (India), Institute of Public Health Bangalore (India), the M S Swaminathan Research Foundation (India) and the University of Melbourne (Australia) between September 2025 and August 2028.

RtR NSA partners pledge to contribute to the goal, share and implement clear plans towards achieving it, and publicly report progress using the metrics framework developed by the RtR team. titles: Equipment Support for Health Training Institutions (ESHTIs)
descriptions: Nigeria has the third worst maternal and under-5 mortality rates in the world. One of the biggest constraints to tackling this is the chronic shortage of health workers – with 3.5 doctors per 10,000 people (vs. 30 in the UK), and 15 nurses and midwives per 10,000 people (vs. 90 in the UK). titles: Engaging Inter-Religious Harmony Forum in Conflict Transformation and Peacebuilding
descriptions: While religious freedom is guaranteed in our Constitution, Indonesia continues to struggle with religious conflicts that harm religious minorities. An increasingly popular strategy in dealing with such conflict is mediation, most notably by the Inter-Religious Harmony Forums (FKUB). Although the use of this non-legal mechanism is perceived to be less costly, less divisive, and more sustainable, mediations by FKUB have been criticized for undermining minority rights. This is because mediation is often misunderstood and misused as a way to “legally” force the minority to succumb to the majority’s demand. The project aims to strengthen local FKUB members and inter-faith leaders by (1) building the mediation skills and knowledge of FKUB members, (2) facilitating them to collaborate with other relevant actors for effective conflict resolution, and (3) developing participatory community processes and forums that can help to build social capital, overcome mistrust, and set a framework for constructive disputes resolution.

titles: [No Longer in Use] Enhancing democratic resilience through open society in Indonesia
descriptions:
This project aims to support inclusive governance and institutional collaboration in Indonesia by drawing on relevant expertise from the United Kingdom. It focuses on three key areas: stakeholder engagement, technical assistance, and open government.

The first area involves fostering constructive dialogue and collaboration among Parliament, government institutions, and civil society. Through multi-stakeholder discussions and policy exchanges, the project will help strengthen relationships and promote shared learning. A Reform Observatory will be established to provide a platform for civil society to contribute to discussions on governance and electoral processes. Policy dialogues between the United Kingdom and Indonesia will be designed around mutual interests and priorities.

The second area provides tailored technical assistance to enhance the capacity of public institutions and civil society on topics such as governance, justice systems, elections, and public accountability. This includes support for evidence-based policymaking through tools like regulatory impact assessments and cost-benefit analyses. The project will also help identify opportunities to improve transparency and access to public information, particularly in the context of electoral data.

The third area supports the development of Indonesia’s next Open Government National Action Plan and a broader strategy for open governance. This includes facilitating policy consultations and encouraging collaboration across government bodies to strengthen public service delivery and citizen engagement. Longer-term efforts in this area will be supported through complementary regional initiatives.
The project will engage a wide range of stakeholders, including parliamentary bodies, government ministries, political parties, and civil society organisations, ensuring that participation is inclusive and relevant to each area of work.

titles: Ukraine Humanitarian Response and Early Recovery 2025-2026 (FCDO III)
descriptions:
In response to continued humanitarian needs and consequent impact of the conflict in Ukraine, this project will build upon the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) activities funded by FCDO from 2023 to 2025 and BRC bilateral funding. Expressed through a new FCDO MoU, funding will support the URCS emergency response and disaster management capacities as well as their medium to long-term ambitions as expressed through their ‘One Plan’.
 
In alignment with BRC and URCS strategies, the FCDO 25/26 project has been designed in close collaboration with URCS, with all activities aligned with the URCS One Plan. BRC has a wider programmatic engagement with URCS that is supported by bilateral funding from its Ukraine Appeal. Activities within this programme will support elements of this project.

FCDO III 2025-26 is a key component of the BRC-URCS programme and is viewed as a step towards a longer-term funding relationship that will ensure the sustainability of URCS over the next three to five years. This project therefore seeks to balance investment in immediate humanitarian needs with activities that underpin the capacity and strategic ambitions of the URCS and contribute to greater resilience and early recovery.

In response to learnings from 2023 to present, this project has been designed to include more effective targeting of activities, aligned with a more focused technical approach and ability to show outcomes.  Cash assistance will be a key modality to achieving objectives involving relief and recovery efforts, and a main cost driver amounting to approximately 40% of the project budget.

titles: Responsible and Inclusive Business Programme: Ukraine Business Compact
descriptions: The project will strengthen the capacity of the UNGC Network in Ukraine and Government of Ukraine to promote the Ukraine Business Compact. This will give leading national and international businesses a platform to demonstrate their support for Responsible Business Conduct principles when engaging in Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction. The Governments of the UK and Ukraine co-hosted Ukraine Recovery Conference (URC23) in London in June 2023, which aimed to mobilize the international community to help secure Ukraine’s long-term economic future, including helping Ukraine build back better, as a more resilient, greener, and more prosperous European nation. In particular, the URC23 placed emphasis on the strength and potential role of the private sector – and the reforms required to drive investment – as essential components of Ukraine’s long-term recovery, in its drive to modernise, build a resilient and agile economy and emerge from war as a stronger and more prosperous state. The Ukraine Business Compact (UBC) was launched at URC23 to reinforce the business community’s support for peace in in Ukraine and to set out mutual expectations for the success of recovery efforts. The Compact now has the co-secretariat of UNGCU and the Tony Blair Institute (TBI). It is crucial to actively engage and maintain the interest of international businesses both in identifying opportunities for companies to engage and invest in Ukraine, and also to support the government of Ukraine in reform implementation. Facilitating a constructive dialogue between the Government of Ukraine and the private sector is key to achieving this. The UBC is a readymade initiative to help facilitate dialogue between a broad range of private sector institutions and the government of Ukraine on these key issues.
